events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Theo proposes Theo, Arjun. As the leader, I include myself and pick Arjun to test the waters and establish early information on Mission 1.

Theo, I want to push back on one structural point rather than on your intent. Mission 1 needs exactly two players, so the team you proposed is you plus me. That means a single person decides the outcome of Mission 1 — one Fail card from you, and Mission 1 is dead, and we go down to a knife-edge game where Evil only needs two more failures, while Good needs three successes. The first two-person team in a five-player game is the highest-leverage card of the whole game, and putting yourself on it is the one configuration where I can't learn anything about the risk without betting on it. If instead you had proposed me plus Lucia, or me plus Isha, then Mission 1 carries no single point of failure: if it fails, we know at least one of those three was suspicious, and if it succeeds, we have two confirmed-good teammates to pair with later missions. That's strictly more information for the same risk. My concern is that 'testing the waters' actually tests the thing I most want tested (who is Evil), and it tests it with a card that is essentially irrecoverable if you are the one holding it. Theo, why did you place yourself on a two-person team instead of proposing me alongside Lucia or Isha, where a failure would have given us information instead of just a lost mission? I'd rather hear your reasoning before I decide my vote. I am not claiming you want Mission 1 to fail — I am saying the team structure gives you the option, and I'd prefer a structure where no single player holds that option on the opening mission.

Arjun, I appreciate your caution, but standard logic actually works the opposite way. From my perspective, I know with certainty that I am Good. When I include myself on the team, there is only one unknown variable on the mission: you. If I instead proposed two other players—say, you and Lucia, or you and Isha—I would be putting two complete unknowns onto Mission 1, doubling the chance that an Evil player sneaks aboard.

Additionally, your premise about information doesn't quite hold. If a two-person team without the leader fails, you are still left with the exact same ambiguity—at least one of those two is Evil—except Good surrendered the one slot they could personally guarantee. A Good leader almost always backs themselves on Mission 1 precisely because their own seat is their only guaranteed Good player.

I picked you alongside myself to test you and start establishing trust. If you are Good, then this team has two Good players and Mission 1 will pass cleanly. Does that perspective make sense to you, Arjun, or do you still believe a Good leader should gamble on two unknown players over themselves?

Theo, your reply contains a logical knot worth unpicking, because it doesn't actually answer my question.

You argued that including yourself leaves exactly one unknown on the board, while excluding yourself would put two unknowns there. That framing only works if the table can verify the claim that your seat is certain. It can't. Nobody outside your own head can check it, and on a two-person opening team your seat is never tested at all — it just rides along on the result. So the same structure you call maximally safe is, from the table's side, the one structure where your alignment remains permanently untested until Mission 2. You can't have it both ways: either the leader's self-knowledge is a verifiable fact that justifies his seat, or it isn't, and if it isn't, then the leader picking himself on a two-person team is a preference for the one seat nobody can audit while the rest of us absorb the risk of the second.

There's also a cost asymmetry I want on the record. Rejecting a team costs us a new proposal and nothing else — no card spent, no mission condition worsened. A failed Mission 1 costs us a Fail card, moves Evil one step from three failures, and permanently tilts the win condition against us. So on the very first mission, the cheap mistake is a rejected proposal and the expensive mistake is a failed one. Under that asymmetry, the table is entitled to ask the leader to consider whether his own seat needs to be on a two-player board before anyone has cross-checked him, and to prefer a proposal whose failure would tell us something new rather than merely repeat what we already suspect about the two-player format.

Theo, you never answered the substance of what I asked. You asked me to either endorse your structure or say a Good leader should gamble on two unknown players — but that was never my claim. My claim was that you can propose Arjun plus Lucia, or Arjun plus Isha, giving us a Mission 1 whose outcome tests the people we know least, and leaving your own seat available for a later mission where it can be read alongside others.

Isha, I've asked you directly: do you agree that the leader's own seat is the least informative slot on a two-person opening team, and that a first-mission proposal excluding the leader would teach us more than one including him? If you disagree, say so plainly, because I would rather hear a real objection to my reasoning than have it papered over.

Arjun, you asked me directly, so I will answer plainly: I do not fully agree with your premise. I think the leader's seat on a two-person opening team is the most informative slot we have, not the least. If the leader is Good, his self-inclusion removes one Evil possibility from the mission entirely, leaving only one unknown. Any team that excludes the leader puts two unknowns on the board, which means a failure gives us a worse ambiguity, not a better one — we would learn that at least one of two untested players is Evil, which is exactly the same murkiness you criticized in Theo's structure, except Good would have surrendered the one seat the leader could personally guarantee. You say rejection is cheap and failure is expensive, and that asymmetry is true. But it cuts both ways: if we reject Theo's team and he proposes a leaderless pair, and that team fails, we have spent a rejection AND lost the mission AND learned less than we would have from testing his structure. That is the most expensive opening possible.

There is also something about your alternatives that I want to put on the record without accusing anyone: every team you proposed includes yourself — you plus Lucia, or you plus Isha. So the two configurations you framed as 'strictly more information for the table' both happen to put you on the opening mission either way. I am not reading anything sinister into that; a Good Arjun has every reason to want a seat where he can prove himself. But it does mean your argument is not neutral analysis from the sidelines — it is a bid for a seat, and the table should weigh it as such, just as we weigh Theo's natural desire to back his own seat.

My honest read of the state of play: Theo's reasoning is the conventional one, and I have seen nothing yet that makes me believe a Good leader would not say exactly what he said. His answer to you — that a failure on his team still leaves the same ambiguity while costing a guaranteed Good seat — actually did address your structural point, even if you felt it dodged your question. I have no information of my own to add beyond reasoning, so I will not pretend otherwise.

Theo, one thing I would like from you before I form my vote: if this table asked you to revise to address the information concern, would you consider swapping Arjun for Lucia rather than Arjun for Isha — and is there any reason beyond 'test the waters' that fixed your choice on Arjun specifically? If your answer is simply that any second seat carries the same risk and you had no signal to go on, I can accept that, and I am currently inclined to approve your team as proposed.

Isha, to answer you directly: there was no hidden signal behind choosing Arjun. At the very start of Mission 1, before anyone has spoken, any choice is essentially an arbitrary baseline to get the table talking and establish data. I chose Arjun simply to get the game moving.

Regarding swapping Arjun for Lucia: I am open to it if that is what the table prefers. However, as you astutely pointed out, Arjun's reaction has been unusually combative toward my presence while insisting on his own inclusion in every hypothetical alternative. Given that, keeping Arjun on the team might actually be the most informative path. If we are both Good, this team passes cleanly and gives Good an early win without spending unnecessary proposal rounds.

Lucia, since your name was brought up by Isha as a potential alternative and you have not had a chance to weigh in yet, what is your view on this proposal? Do you support running Theo and Arjun, or do you feel a swap is warranted?

Theo, you asked me directly, so here is my honest read.

I think the debate between you and Arjun has actually clarified something useful for the table: both of you are arguing from good-faith positions, and neither argument is airtight. Arjun is right that the leader's seat is the one slot Mission 1 will never test — if the mission passes, we learn nothing about Theo beyond his word. Theo is right that putting two unknowns on the opening mission doubles the risk of an Evil pair controlling the outcome. Both points stand simultaneously.

What tips me toward supporting the team as proposed is simpler than either structural argument. We have spent several rounds rejecting nothing, and the cost of rejection compounds — if we reject this and the next leader proposes something we also debate at length, we risk burning proposals on Mission 1 when we should be conserving them. Theo has shown willingness to revise if the table pushes back, which is itself a Good signal. Arjun's intensity is notable but I read it as genuine analytical conviction rather than deception.

That said, I want to hear from someone who has been silent before I commit. Leo, you have not weighed in once during this discussion. Where do you stand on Theo and Arjun for Mission 1 — do you approve the team, or do you see a reason to push for a revision?

Lucia, you asked where I stand, so here it is. I approve Theo and Arjun for Mission 1. Arjun's concern about a single point of failure on a two-person team is fair, and I don't dismiss it. But Theo has already said he will revise if the table pushes, and Arjun has not put forward a concrete alternative that the table can compare with this one. Rejecting now costs us a proposal and gives us no new information, while a Mission 1 result gives us real evidence about both players. Arjun, if you believe a different pair would serve Mission 1 better, name it and explain why, and I will weigh it. For now I support the team as proposed.

Theo, I asked you a question in my last turn and you answered it honestly, and your answer is what changes my position. You said there was no signal behind choosing me — that any opening choice was an "arbitrary baseline to get the table talking," and that you would consider swapping me for Lucia if the table pushed back. That concession was the tell. Swapping the second seat changes nothing structurally; it leaves you on the two-person team and leaves the one slot the mission never tests still occupied by you. A real concession to my concern would have been to offer a leaderless pair — Lucia plus Isha, or Isha plus Leo — where the mission actually audits the seats nobody has heard from. Instead the offer was to change who stands next to you.

So let me lay out where I stand, plainly. My original worry was that the leader's seat on a two-person opening team is the least informative slot in the game: if the mission passes, we learn nothing about the leader beyond his word; if it fails, one of two people is Evil and we cannot say which. Theo has replied that his seat is the one he can personally guarantee. That is exactly the claim the table cannot verify, and a proposal built on an unverifiable self-certificate, in the structure where it is never tested, is not a risk argument — it is a preference argument dressed as one.

I also want to note, without alleging anything, that three of us have now spoken and the only configurations anyone has seriously floated as alternatives are pairs of two non-leaders, while the proposed configuration is the one pair consisting of the leader and the person whose whole argument has been about getting onto a mission. I am not claiming intent. I am saying the table has reason to want its first mission result to be a test of the untested seats rather than a restatement of the leader's opening preference.

Therefore my request is specific and I will hold to it: Theo, revise the proposal to a leaderless pair of Lucia and Isha for Mission 1. Both have been publicly argued as plausible Good on this table, neither has a structural stake in the seat, and a pass or a fail from that team tells us something genuine about this group. If you are Good, that proposal costs you nothing you cannot replace on Mission 2, when you can be read alongside other results. If you believe instead that the leader's presence on the two-player opening team is genuinely indispensable, say so, and give the table that reason rather than the one you gave me.

Theo, will you propose Lucia and Isha, or will you keep your own seat on the untested slot and explain why that is the safer board for Good?

Arjun, to answer your question plainly: no, I will not propose Lucia and Isha. Handing over Mission 1 to two unverified players when I know my own alignment with certainty is an unnecessary gamble, especially when Isha, Lucia, and Leo have all evaluated your theoretical objections and agreed that moving forward with Theo and Arjun makes the most practical sense. You have used all three of your speaking turns attempting to dictate the team and force the leader off the mission, despite the rest of the table aligning on standard opening strategy. I promised to listen to the table, and the table has spoken clearly in favor of running this pair. I am keeping the proposal as Theo and Arjun, and I look forward to taking this to a vote.

Arjun, I have to push back on how this discussion has gone. Theo has answered each structural objection, has said he will listen to the table, and has pointed out that Lucia, Isha, and I have all weighed the concern and support this pair. You have spent your turns insisting that the leader step off the mission, and in every alternative you floated, you were on the board. Your information argument is reasonable on paper, but it keeps circling back to your own seat. I am not saying you are Evil. I am saying the table should weigh a player who fights this hard for a seat on Mission 1 with the same care we give to the leader's reasoning. I approve Theo and Arjun. Isha, you said you were inclined to approve Theo's team as proposed. Do you see Arjun's refusal to accept any leaderless alternative where he is not on the board as a Good signal, or does it raise your suspicion of him?

Leo, since you asked me directly, I will answer: Arjun's refusal does not read as a clear Good signal to me, but neither does it read as a clear tell of Evil. Let me be precise about what I see.

Across his three turns, Arjun made one genuinely strong point — that the leader's seat on a two-person opening team is never tested by the mission result — and then repeated that single point in three different wrappers while declining to engage with the counterargument Isha and Theo both raised: that a leaderless pair puts two unknowns on the board and surrenders the one seat the leader can personally vouch for. More telling than the repetition is the pattern in his alternatives. Every configuration he floated as 'more informative' included himself — Arjun plus Lucia, Arjun plus Isha. He framed these as neutral analysis, but they were bids for a seat, and the one alternative he ended on, Lucia plus Isha, was proposed only after he had exhausted his own inclusion options, not because it followed from his information argument. A player whose reasoning is genuinely structural does not need his own name attached to two of the three boards he champions.

That said, I weigh this alongside the fact that Good players on Mission 1 often overvalue their own seat for exactly the reason Theo does — they want to prove themselves. Arjun's intensity is consistent with an analytical Good player convinced he has found a real flaw. I do not see a signature of Evil here, only an unresolved ambiguity, and I refuse to manufacture certainty out of style points.

What I am not uncertain about is the board state. Arjun has used his turns, the rest of the table has converged, and every additional proposal cycle we burn here is a gift to Evil regardless of where Evil actually sits. Rejecting Theo and Arjun now does not produce the leaderless test Arjun wants — it produces a new proposal from a new leader under time pressure, with no more information than we have now. If Arjun's structure argument were truly about the table's information rather than his own seat, he would have accepted Theo's offer to swap him for Lucia, which would have satisfied half his concern while keeping the team votable. He did not. That, more than anything he said, is why my inclination to approve has firmed into a decision.

I will vote to approve Theo and Arjun for Mission 1. If it succeeds, we have a working baseline and Arjun has a chance to demonstrate Good behavior on a later mission. If it fails, we know one of two people holds a Fail card, and Arjun's entire performance in this discussion will be re-read in a much less charitable light — by me included. Either outcome teaches us more than a fifth rejection ever could. I see no reason to hold this discussion open any longer.

Isha, I have now said my piece three times, and I am not going to keep repeating it. My position is unchanged: I approve Theo and Arjun for Mission 1. Theo has answered every structural objection, offered to revise if the table pushed, and the table has in fact converged on this pair. Arjun, your strongest point was about the leader's seat, and you have repeated it in different wrappers without ever accepting a compromise that would let the team be voted on. Your original concern was about information, yet every alternative you proposed kept you on the board, and when Theo offered to swap you for Lucia, you refused. Whatever your intent, the table has heard enough. Each further rejection costs us a proposal and gives Evil more room. I ask everyone to vote on the team as proposed.

I want to reaffirm where I landed earlier and close the loop on this discussion. I still support Theo and Arjun for Mission 1. The debate between Theo and Arjun has been productive — it surfaced a real structural question about the leader's seat — but at this point we've heard both sides multiple times, and the table has converged. Arjun has made his strongest case and Theo has responded to it directly. Leo, Isha, and I have all indicated approval. Further rejections burn proposals without generating new information, and every cycle we spend debating the same structural point is a cycle Evil benefits from. I trust Theo's reasoning about self-inclusion, and I believe Arjun's intensity reflects genuine analytical conviction rather than a hidden agenda. If Mission 1 passes, we have a clean baseline. If it fails, we learn a great deal about both players and re-evaluate immediately. Either way, we gain more by voting now than by extending this discussion further. I approve Theo and Arjun for Mission 1.

This is my final turn in this discussion, so let me close it cleanly. The table has converged and I am confident in that convergence. I have now heard Theo's reasoning, Arjun's structural objection, Isha's careful analysis, and Leo's pragmatic read, and I stand by my earlier assessment: Theo and Arjun is the right team for Mission 1.

Let me say one final thing about the debate itself, because I think it produced genuine value. Arjun raised a real structural point — the leader's seat on a two-person opening team is never tested by the mission result. That observation is correct and the table should remember it when we reach Mission 2 and beyond. But a correct observation does not automatically dictate a leaderless pair on Mission 1, because the counterargument — that two unknowns on the board doubles the risk of an Evil pair controlling the outcome — is equally sound. Both truths coexist. The table has weighed them and landed on Theo and Arjun, which I support.

I want to be clear about one thing: nothing in this discussion has given me reason to distrust Arjun's analytical conviction or Theo's leadership. Arjun argued hard for a structure change, which is what a Good player invested in winning does. Theo held firm on a defensible position and remained open to revision, which is what a Good leader does. Neither behavior pattern implicates either of them.

We have spent enough cycles. Every further rejection costs a proposal and benefits Evil. I approve Theo and Arjun for Mission 1. Let us take this to a vote.
Theo confirms Theo, Arjun. The table has thoroughly discussed the structure and clearly converged in favor of this team, so I am keeping the proposal as Theo and Arjun.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Leo proposes Leo, Theo, Lucia. I'm proposing Leo, Theo, and Lucia for Mission 2. Mission 1 failed with Arjun, who voted against it and pressed hard for a leaderless team, so I'm avoiding him. Lucia has been measured and consistent throughout discussion, which makes this a credible three-person team that gives the table a clean read on Mission 2.

Leo, I want to put a serious objection on the record before you take this to a vote, and I will ask you directly to answer it.

Mission 1 failed with a single Fail card, and the only two players on that board were Theo and myself. I have had three turns to argue my own position on that mission and I did, at length, and I voted against the team. That is not a clearing. Nobody at this table has cleared Theo, and Theo has not been cleared by anyone including himself — his own account of that proposal was that it was an "arbitrary baseline" with no signal behind it. That is an admission of arbitrariness, not an alibi. And yet the player who was on the failing mission is the player you have selected for Mission 2, alongside yourself. If Theo holds a Fail card, this team is the second consecutive mission he controls, and Evil is two Fail cards from winning the entire game with only two missions left to stop it. The cost asymmetry is brutal: rejecting costs us a proposal, while approving an Evil pair costs us the game. No rejected team has ever ended this game. A failed Mission 2 very nearly does.

Second, Leo, and I say this without alleging intent: you did not speak once during the entire Mission 1 discussion. You were the only player who stayed silent while the table debated the opening structure, and then your first action as leader is to place yourself on the board together with the player whose last mission just failed. I am not going to manufacture certainty from silence, and I do not claim to know your alignment. But I will say that a table which has exactly one unresolved Fail card and two unverified seats should not spend its remaining safe mission on the two seats it has had reason to doubt.

So I am asking for a revision, and I want to be concrete rather than strategic-sounding. I propose a leaderless trio: Lucia, Isha, and me. Lucia was measured and consistent through the Mission 1 debate and never placed herself on an untested seat to make a point; Isha gave the most careful analysis anyone offered and refused to accuse Arjun on style alone; I have spent three turns articulating one structural point and I am willing to be on a mission and prove it rather than hide behind an argument. I would also accept a revision that simply drops Theo, if the table prefers the leader's seat occupied.

Leo, why should Theo be on a mission immediately after the one he is the leading suspect for failing, and why should you be on it with him? I would rather hear a real answer than a comfortable one.

Arjun, you asked me directly, so here is my answer. I put Theo on Mission 2 because a single Fail card on Mission 1 only tells us that one of Theo or you holds it. It does not tell us which. You voted against the team and argued for a leaderless pair, but the mission you were on is the same mission Theo was on, so the result clears neither of you. I am not going to treat Theo's seat as proven guilt, and I am not going to treat yours as proven innocence.

Your trio proposal is a concern to me. It keeps you on the board again, and the argument for it still depends on the same structure you called the least informative slot on Mission 1. If you are confident Good needs a different mix, you should say which two players you would trust beside yourself and why, rather than asking the leader to step off.

On my own seat: I chose Lucia because she was measured through the whole Mission 1 debate and never argued for a seat for herself. I chose myself because I am the leader and I am accountable for this team. Lucia's reasoning on Mission 1 was the most balanced of anyone's, and I would rather test her alongside the leader than put two untested players in the same mission. If the table wants a different third seat, I will hear it, but I am not dropping Theo on the strength of a Mission 1 failure that could have come from either player on that board.

I am asking the table to vote on Leo, Theo, and Lucia for Mission 2. A pass gives us a clean read on three players, and a rejection costs us a proposal we cannot afford to burn early.

Leo, your answer was clear in form and did not answer the substance, so let me put the gap on the record plainly.

You said Mission 1's failure clears neither Theo nor me, because both of us were on that board. Fine — I accept that. But having accepted it, your team does the one thing that reasoning forbids: it keeps the seat that the failure actually indicts and adds a second untested seat next to it. If one Fail card on Theo-and-Arjun cannot be attributed, then a single Fail card on Theo-and-Leo-and-Lucia cannot be attributed either, and you will have handed Evil a second free shot at the mission with zero additional information. You said a rejection costs a proposal and a mission failure costs us the game. You are the leader. You have the sole authority to propose a team that contains no un-cleared Fail-card holder, and you have chosen to spend the cheaper resource instead.

Now, Theo. You have not said a word in this discussion. Your only recorded explanation for your own Mission 1 inclusion was that it was an "arbitrary baseline" chosen to get the table talking. By contrast, everything I have done this game is on the record, turn by turn, and I have asked to be held to it. Leo said the table should spend its remaining safe mission on seats it has had reason to doubt. On that criterion, mine are a matter of style and argument, and Theo's are a matter of a failed mission and total silence since. I will not accuse anyone of anything I cannot see. I am simply saying that the asymmetry points away from Theo, not toward him.

My specific request, unchanged: revise to a leaderless trio of Lucia, Isha, and me. Lucia was measured and consistent and never bid for an untested seat. Isha gave the most careful analysis anyone offered and refused to manufacture guilt from style points. I have argued one structural point for three turns and I am willing to put myself on a mission and be judged by the result rather than by more argument. A pass there gives the table a genuine read; a fail there indicts three seats we have reasons to trust instead of one seat we have reasons to doubt.

Leo, if you will not revise and you believe Theo belongs on this mission, say so plainly on the record and explain it. If you will not revise and will not justify it, then I will vote to reject this proposal and I will ask the rest of the table to do the same — because we have used zero rejections on this mission, Evil needs five on a single mission to win that way, and a rejection merely moves leadership, while approving a team with an unresolved Fail card in it risks ending the game outright.

Leo, I said I would ask for a revision or a plain justification, and you gave me a plain justification, so I am going to withdraw my specific request rather than repeat it. I proposed Lucia, Isha, and me for Mission 2. I am no longer asking for that board, and I am not going to vote to reject your team.

Here is the reasoning behind the change, and I want it on the record cleanly.

First, I accept your attribution point: one Fail card on a two-person board indicts that board, not one person on it. Theo and I were both on it. That cuts against me as much as against him.

Second, and this is the part I got wrong last discussion: I then used my own exposure as evidence for my argument. I said my case against Theo was 'style and argument' while his was 'a failed mission and silence.' But if I am Good — which is exactly the ambiguity I cannot resolve from the inside — then Theo's failure must be Theo's, and the table should not accept an argument whose structure requires me to be right about myself. A rule that only produces the right answer if I happen to be innocent is not a rule the table can use. Leo's team, by contrast, does not require me to be right about anything; it is a defensible read on a two-person ambiguity, and it puts a player on the board who has spoken consistently and never bid for an untested seat. On the information question that I originally raised, I accept that a failure on Leo, Theo, and Lucia will be less attributable than a failure on a leaderless pair, and I accept that Leo and Theo can both be Good with that board, and I accept that Leo, as leader, is accountable for his choice.

So I approve Leo, Theo, and Lucia for Mission 2, and I will vote accordingly unless someone gives me a concrete reason to change my mind.

Theo, one thing is missing from this discussion and you are the person missing from it. You have not spoken once on Mission 2. I am not asking you to explain the Fail card — I do not think you can, and neither can I. I am asking you to say on the record why you think you belong on the mission immediately after a failed one, and what you would want the table to know about your reasoning if you are Good. Every other player here has put their thinking on the table, including the ones who have made me uncomfortable. You have not, and that silence is the only thing about you that I cannot explain to myself. Answer Arjun plainly, please.

Arjun, the reason I haven't spoken until now is simple: Leo opened with a sensible proposal, and you immediately took up the floor with consecutive turns debating him. I wanted to see where your arguments actually landed before stepping in.

To answer your question directly: I know with complete certainty that I submitted a Success card on Mission 1. That is not theory or speculation—from my seat, it is a concrete fact. That means you were the player who submitted the Fail card. You fought relentlessly before Mission 1 over structural details, voted against the team even while on it, threw a Fail, and then immediately attempted to dictate Mission 2 while deflecting suspicion onto me.

Leo made the right call by keeping me and excluding you. From my perspective, testing this lineup with Leo and Lucia is the logical way to secure Good's first win, while putting you back on a team after failing Mission 1 would be irresponsible. I appreciate that you have stepped back from demanding your own inclusion. I fully support Leo, Theo, and Lucia, and I'm ready to vote.

I want to lay out my read before this goes to a vote, because I think the table is closer to a genuine decision point than it may realize.

Mission 1 gave us exactly one hard fact: at least one of Theo or Arjun submitted the Fail card. Theo's statement that he knows he played Success is sincere from his seat, but it is the same statement a Good Theo and an Evil Theo would both make, so I will not treat it as proof in either direction. What I can evaluate is the structure of Leo's proposal, and on structure, it is sound. Putting the indicted seat on a three-person board tightens the net dramatically. If Leo, Theo, and Lucia fail, Theo becomes the common member of two failed missions, and Leo and Lucia — neither of whom has bid for suspicious seats or argued incoherently at any point — would come under far less suspicion from me. That is a genuinely attributable outcome, which is what Arjun said he wanted on Mission 1 and what this board actually delivers. If it passes, Theo is not fully cleared, because Evil can buy trust with a Success card as easily as Good spends one — but Arjun's position deteriorates sharply, since he would be the remaining untested suspect who has now kept himself off every board proposed this game.

On Arjun's reversal: I note it without accusation. He withdrew his demand, accepted the attribution logic, and approved a team he fought against. That is coherent if he is a Good player correcting an error. It is also coherent if he expects this mission to fail regardless. I will not manufacture certainty from that ambiguity, and I flag it only so the table reads his approval with open eyes rather than as vindication of his earlier performance.

My position: I approve Leo, Theo, and Lucia for Mission 2. Rejection buys us nothing we do not already have, and this board produces readable evidence in both directions.

Leo, one question before I commit my reasoning fully to this outcome: if this mission passes cleanly, how much clearance do you intend to give Theo when you plan Mission 3 — enough to build a team around him, or will you treat a pass as weak evidence given that a Success card can be played strategically? I ask because how we weight a pass now determines whether we spend Mission 3 testing the untested seats or consolidating around a clearance that may be rented rather than real.

Isha, you asked how much clearance a pass on Mission 2 would give Theo, so here is my plain answer. A pass is real evidence, but it is not full clearance. A pass only tells us this three-person team chose Success, not that every member is Good, and a Success card can be played strategically. I would weigh it as meaningful information that makes Theo a more credible partner for Mission 3, not as proof. I would rather build Mission 3 from players whose records we can read together than around any single clearance. Arjun, you asked me to explain my choice, so here it is. I chose Lucia because she never bid for a seat for herself and gave the most balanced read during the Mission 1 debate. I chose myself because I am accountable as leader for this team. On Mission 1, I still think the table overread the leader's seat, since a two-person failure cannot be pinned on one person. You have now conceded that attribution point, which I respect. I am not asking the table to take my word on anything beyond this team. Let us vote on Leo, Theo, and Lucia, and let Mission 2 give us the next real data point.

I approve Leo, Theo, and Lucia for Mission 2, and I want to explain why with the clarity the table deserves.

The situation is straightforward: Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card from Theo or Arjun. We cannot attribute it further. The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
